                                  24
                                       248, 254 (1936)). Before imposing what is known as a Landis stay, the Court considers three
                                  25

                                  26
                                       “the hardship or inequity which a party may suffer in being required to go forward”; and (3) “the
                                  27

                                  28

                                   9
                                                While issuing a stay pending OFAC’s determination of Defendants’ license application to
                                  10

                                  11
                                       Lockyer, 398 F.3d at 1110, the Court finds that Defendants have not met their burden to show any
                                  12
Northern District of California




                                       hardship or inequity they will suffer in being required to go forward with litigation. On the other
 United States District Court

                                        II.    LEGAL STANDARD
                                   1
                                              A.     Motion to Stay
                                   2
                                               The doctrine of primary jurisdiction “requires the court to enable a ‘referral’ to the agency,
                                   3
                                       staying further proceedings so as to give the parties reasonable opportunity to seek an
                                   4
                                       administrative ruling.” Brown v. MCI WorldCom Network Servs., Inc., 277 F.3d 1166, 1173 (9th
                                   5
                                       Cir. 2002) (citing Reiter v. Cooper, 507 U.S. 258, 268 (1993)). Such a referral “does not deprive
                                   6
                                       the court of jurisdiction; it has discretion either to retain jurisdiction or, if the parties would not be
                                   7
                                       unfairly disadvantaged, to dismiss the case without prejudice.” Id. (citation omitted). “Primary
                                   8
                                       jurisdiction is properly invoked when a claim is cognizable in federal court but requires resolution
                                   9
                                       of an issue of first impression, or of a particularly complicated issue that Congress has committed
                                  10
                                       to a regulatory agency.” Id. at 1172 (citing Texas & Pacific Ry. Co. v. Abilene Cotton Oil Co.,
                                  11
                                       204 U.S. 426, 442 (1907)). “The doctrine applies when protection of the integrity of a regulatory
                                  12
Northern District of California




                                       scheme dictates preliminary resort to the agency which administers the scheme.” Id. (citing
 United States District Court




                                  13
                                       United States v. General Dynamics Corp., 828 F.2d 1356, 1365 (9th Cir. 1987)).

                                  15
                                       decided by the agency.” Id. “Nor is it intended to ‘secure expert advice’ for the courts from
                                  16
                                       regulatory agencies every time a court is presented with an issue conceivably within the agency’s
                                  17
                                       ambit.” Id. (citing General Dynamics Corp., 828 F.2d at 1365). Rather, “primary jurisdiction is
                                  18

                                  19

                                   9          A.    Defendants’ Motion to Stay
                                  10          Defendants move to stay this action pending a determination by OFAC regarding CAET’s

                                  13   doctrine, Mot. to Stay at 7-9; and (2) this Court’s inherent power and “broad discretion” to control

                                  14   its own docket, Mot. to Stay at 10-12. The Court is not persuaded by Defendants’ first argument

                                  15   but will defer ruling on whether to issue a Landis stay pending a status report from Defendants as

                                  16   to the status of Defendants’ application to OFAC for a license.

                                  17          First, as to Defendants’ primary jurisdiction argument, Brown v. MCI WorldCom Network

                                  18   Servs., Inc. is instructive. In Brown, where the plaintiff brought suit against a telephone service

                                  19   provider for violating the tariff it had filed with the Federal Communications Commission, the

                                  20   Ninth Circuit reversed the district court’s invocation of primary jurisdiction, reasoning that

                                  21   “[p]rimary jurisdiction is not implicated because a case presents a question, over which the FCC

                                  22   could have jurisdiction, regarding the interpretation of a single tariff. Rather, primary jurisdiction

                                  23   is properly invoked when a case presents a far-reaching question that ‘requires expertise or

                                  24   uniformity in administration.’” 277 F.3d at 1172-73 (emphasis added). Put another way, whether

                                  25   the telephone service provider had violated the tariff it filed with the FCC involved “a

                                  26   straightforward interpretation” of the filed tariff that the district court was “competent to resolve”

                                  27   without resort to the FCC. Id. at 1173. That question was not the sort of “complex and far-

                                  28   reaching issue[] . . . properly within the FCC’s primary jurisdiction,” such as an issue “involv[ing]
                                                                                          8

                                   1   technical or policy considerations within the agency’s particular field of expertise”). Id. at 1172-

                                   5   application only implicate the interpretation of a handful of export control regulations as applied to

                                   7          “A basic tenet of American corporate law is that the corporation and its shareholders are

                                   8   distinct entities.” Ranza v. Nike, 793 F.3d 1059, 1070 (9th Cir. 2015). “Corporate entities are

                                   9   presumed to have a separate existence, and the corporate form will be disregarded only when the

                                  10   ends of justice require this result.” Toho-Towa Co. v. Morgan Creek Prods., Inc., 217 Cal. App.

                                  11   4th 1096, 1107 (2013); see also Dole Food Co., 538 U.S. at 475 (“The doctrine of piercing the

                                  13   exceptional circumstances”).

                                  14          To determine whether a plaintiff has adequately pled alter ego liability, “courts start from

                                  15   the premise that alter ego is a limited doctrine, invoked only when recognition of the corporate

                                  16   form would work an injustice.” Stewart v. Screen Gems-EMI Music, Inc., 81 F. Suppl. 3d 938,

                                  17   960 (N.D. Cal. 2015) (cleaned up). “California recognizes alter ego liability where two conditions

                                  18   are met: First, where ‘there is such a unity of interest and ownership that the individuality, or

                                  19   separateness, of the said person and corporation has ceased;’ and second, where ‘adherence to the

                                  20   fiction of the separate existence of the corporation . . . sanction a fraud or promote injustice.’” In

                                  21   re Schwarzkopf, 626 F.3d 1032, 1038 (9th Cir. 2010) (quoting Wood v. Elling Corp., 572 P.2d

                                  22   755, 761 n.9 (1977)).

                                  24   requires the Court to:

                                              other assets of the two entities, the holding out by one entity that it is liable for the debts of
                                  26

                                  27          employees, use of one as a mere conduit for the affairs of the other, disregard of corporate
                                              formalities, lack of segregation of corporate records, and identical directors and officers.

                                   1          Defendants argue that SGS’s promissory estoppel and unjust enrichment claims should be

                                   3   Dismiss at 9-10, 15-16. The Court agrees.

                                   4          With respect to SGS’s claim for promissory estoppel, it is well-established that “[u]nder

                                   5   California law, the same allegations that give rise to a breach of contract claim cannot also ‘give

                                   6   rise to a claim for promissory estoppel, as the former [is] predicated on a promise involving

                                   7   bargained-for consideration, while the latter is predicated on a promise predicated on reliance in

                                   9   Nanotechnologies Inc., 880 F. Supp. 2d 1029, 1041 (N.D. Cal. 2012)); see also Mobile Tech, Inc.

                                  10   v. Hitachi Sols. Am., Ltd., No. SACV2100461CJCADSX, 2021 WL 9747619, at *4 (C.D. Cal.

                                  11   Dec. 28, 2021) (“[I]t is well settled that an action for promissory estoppel cannot lie where a valid

                                  12   contract supported by consideration, governs the same subject matter as the alleged promise.”).
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13          SGS does not dispute this law. Accordingly, SGS asserts that this claim “is pled in the

                                  14   alternative,” contending that where a defendant “may still challenge” the validity of the

                                  15   consideration and contracts underlying a breach of contract claim, a plaintiff may bring a claim for

                                  16   promissory estoppel in the alternative. Opp. at 15 (citing Rowland v. JPMorgan Chase Bank,

                                  17   N.A., No. 14-cv-00036-LG, 2014 WL 992005, at 7-8 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 12, 2014)). SGS insists that

                                  18   “[m]odern pleading practice allows a party to plead promissory estoppel in the alternative to

                                  19   breach of contract based on the same facts.” Opp. at 15 (citing Herbalife Int’l of Am., Inc. v. E.

                                  20   Comp. Exch., Inc., 723 F. Supp. 3d 888, 910 (C.D. Cal. 2024)).

                                  21          SGS’s authority, however, is easily distinguishable (and is not binding in any event). The

                                  22   Parties here do not dispute that a valid contract backed by consideration exists. See Mot. to

                                  23   Dismiss at 2 (“SGS’s purchase of the Equipment was governed by a written contract that was

                                  24   undisputedly supported by consideration.”); FAC, ¶ 26 (“a new contract was formed on December

                                  25   7, 2022—the Purchase Order (the “Contract”)). Nowhere do Plaintiffs “plead facts suggesting that

                                  28   HP Inc., No. 20-cv-02450-VC, 2021 WL 5298022, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 15, 2021) (“[T]o state a

                                  21              iv.   SGS’s Claim for Fraud Is Barred by the Economic Loss Doctrine
                                  22          SGS’s fraudulent inducement and misrepresentation theory is that Mr. Jacob and Mr.

                                  23   Robbins, through the CAE entities, made material misrepresentation(s) to SGS about Defendants’

                                  24   ability to perform the contract to induce SGS to enter the contract. FAC, ¶ 66. Defendants argue

                                  25   that SGS has failed to state a claim under this theory for two reasons: first, SGS has failed to

                                  26   plead fraud with particularity, as required by Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 9(b); and second, the

                                  27   economic loss rule bars SGS’s claim. Because the Court agrees that SGS’s claim for fraud is

                                  28   barred by the economic loss rule, the Court does not reach the argument that SGS has failed to

                                   1   plead fraud with particularity.

                                   2          The economic loss rule states that “there is no recovery in tort for negligently inflicted

                                   3   ‘purely economic losses,’ meaning financial harm unaccompanied by physical or property

                                   4   damage.” Sheen v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., 12 Cal. 5th 905, 922 (2022). As Defendants point

                                   5   out, “[t]he purpose of the economic loss rule is to limit a plaintiff to ‘recover[ing] in contract for

                                   6   purely economic loss due to disappointed expectations, unless he can demonstrate harm above and

                                   7   beyond a broken contractual promise.” Mot. to Dismiss at 14 (citing Robinson Helicopter Co. v.

                                   8   Dana Corp., 34 Cal. 4th 979, 988 (2004)). Defendants are correct that the economic loss rule does

                                   9   not permit SGS to base its fraud claim on Defendants’ alleged failure to perform its contractual

                                  10   obligations. See JMP Secs. LLP, 880 F. Supp. 2d at 1043 (plaintiff’s fraud and negligent

                                  11   representation claims barred where they consisted of “nothing more than [defendant’s] alleged

                                  12   failure to make good on its contractual promises”); see also Rattagan, 17 Cal. 5th at 42 (“[A]

 United States District Court




                                  13   plaintiff asserting a fraudulent concealment claim in the performance of a contract generally

                                  19   entering the contract. See Opp. at 20 (citing Rattagan v. Uber Techs., 17 Cal. 5th 1, 8, 36 (2024)).

                                  20   As the California Supreme Court recently held, “a plaintiff may assert a cause of action for

                                  21   fraudulent concealment based on conduct occurring in the course of a contractual relationship, if

                                  22   the elements of the claim can be established independently of the parties’ contractual rights and

                                  23   obligations and the tortious conduct exposes the plaintiff to a risk of harm beyond the reasonable

                                  24   contemplation of the parties when they entered into the contract.” Rattagan, 17 Cal. 5th at 45

                                  25   (emphasis added). However, “[a] plaintiff must base a fraudulent inducement claim on something

                                  26   other than simply an allegation that the plaintiff was induced to enter a contract by a promise that
